claim: Human tests of intellectual tasks share a positive manifold; Spearman (1904) found a common factor with corrected correlations near 0.78-1.00 in small school samples, and later batteries give g factors correlating .95-1.00.
agent_test: Background vocabulary only; no direct test.

claim: Carroll's three-stratum model (g, about 10 broad abilities, narrow abilities) from 461 data sets is the standard taxonomy; Horn argued for 9-10 broad abilities without g; the g vs broad-abilities debate is not settled. Gap search: McGrew 2023 gives Carroll's 2003 numbers (1 g + 9 broad, g loadings .28-.78); the 461 count is still only secondary ('over 450' in other papers).
agent_test: Use broad-ability labels to tag problem classes in the task router; compare per-class accuracy of scaffold vs plain at equal tokens.

claim: Evidence for g is weaker at high ability: Spearman's law of diminishing returns (r about .7 at IQ<78 vs about .4 at IQ>122; Blum & Holling: 2 SD higher sample gives r about .15 lower). Gap search: on 4,575 open-LLM leaderboard models the top half is not lower in PC1 than the bottom half (59.7% vs 55.9%); Krakauer's epoch fall rests on n of 3-8; SLODR tests are open to scale artefacts.
agent_test: Check g share only on IRT-scaled abilities and with n above 30 per band; floors and ceilings mimic SLODR.

claim: Bifactor models fit batteries better than higher-order models (31 batteries, 1.7M test takers) but the fit gap may be partly a statistical bias; so broad factors beyond g are small in some batteries.
agent_test: Fit bifactor vs higher-order on our own task-by-agent matrix before assigning schema states to ability classes.

claim: Working-memory training does not give reliable far transfer to fluid intelligence (meta-analyses; Jaeggi 2008 not robustly replicated).
agent_test: Do not assume drilling a sub-skill in the scaffold lifts general reasoning; test transfer to held-out classes.

claim: Across 591 de-duplicated LLMs and 12 tests, one general factor explains 65.6% of variance, mean g loading .81, omega hierarchical .94, above the human 40-50%; no separate Gf factor.
agent_test: Replicate on our model pool; compute g share with and without near-duplicate fine-tunes.

claim: The LLM g share depends heavily on sample design: the same author's earlier version with 1,232 leaderboard models gave 85.4%, falling to 65.6% after removing near-duplicates (same arXiv id 2310.11616, v1 vs v3). Gap search: an own test on 4,575 leaderboard models finds PC1 73.5%, and 71.6-73.9% with one model per organisation or per base-model key, so family covariance moves the g share by 1-2 points; task mix and model range explain the 65.6-85% spread better.
agent_test: Report g share only on de-duplicated, family-balanced samples.

claim: Other LLM analyses also find a dominant first factor: 75% (156 models), about 80% PC1 (77 models), 79.3% (metabench, >5000 models), and 90% PC1 on a 5-benchmark core (39 models).
agent_test: Use PC1 score as a cheap capability covariate when comparing scaffold arms.

claim: The general factor is not fixed over time: Krakauer finds PC1 on a 4-benchmark battery peaking at 92-95.5% in 2023-24 and falling to 64% in the latest epoch, with a second eigenvalue 1.88 appearing with reasoning models. Gap search: epoch rows are n=3 (PC1 79%, eig2 1.24), 8 (92%), 7 (80%), 4 (64%, eig2 1.88), so epoch I already has eig2 above 1 and the trend is not monotone.
agent_test: Re-run the factor analysis on reasoning vs non-reasoning arms; check whether the scaffold creates a second factor. Small n (3-8 per epoch), sparse matrix.

claim: LLMs show more than one factor when tasks are diverse: Burnell et al. find 3 factors (reasoning, comprehension, language modelling; 82% cumulative) in 29 LLMs x 27 tasks, with poor fit (CFI .70); Maimon et al. find 8 factors in 60 LLMs x 44 benchmarks.
agent_test: Select task mix so reasoning, comprehension and knowledge are separable; test whether scaffold gains are factor-specific.

claim: Reasoning is a separable factor from size: log model size correlates 0.70 with comprehension, -0.50 with language modelling and 0.08 (CI -0.38 to .52) with reasoning; instruction tuning helps reasoning.
agent_test: Test whether scaffolded small model gains on the reasoning factor but not comprehension, at equal tokens.

claim: Benchmark ability dimensions can predict item-level success (ADeLe: weighted AUROC 0.81-0.84) and many benchmarks fail specificity/sensitivity for the dimension they claim.
agent_test: Label our test items by demand dimension; see whether scaffold benefit scales with demand.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Parameter count predicts the general factor with a nonlinear curve (r=.54, N=577; fast to 10B, plateau 10-20B), and only weakly the knowledge/reading factor (r=.11).
agent_test: Plot scaffold gain against base model size to see where it is largest.

claim: CHC-based AI profiling (Hendrycks et al. 2025) shows jagged profiles: GPT-4 27%, GPT-5 57% of 100; GPT-5 scores 7/10 points on on-the-spot reasoning vs GPT-4 0, long-term memory storage 0 for both (verified in Table 1). Gap search: the 0% in memory storage follows from the protocol (new session, external tools disabled), so it scores the bare model, not a model with a memory scaffold.
agent_test: Score our agent per CHC component; memory storage is the stated bottleneck and matches the schema's memory part.

claim: Human-style abstraction tests show LLM gaps that aggregate scores hide: ConceptARC humans 84% vs best ARC solver about 40 points lower; GPT-4 text RAVEN open QA 0.41; CoT did not reliably help.
agent_test: Run scaffold vs plain on ConceptARC items at equal tokens; compare with CoT.

claim: Flynn-effect gains concentrate in fluid/performance subtests more than g loadings predict; g saturation did not change in an Austrian pilot sample.
agent_test: None; background on whether g is a stable construct.

claim: Factorial invariance of CHC structure across countries holds (WISC-V strict invariance) but does not hold in low-IQ groups for single-factor models.
agent_test: None; boundary condition for assuming one structure across ability levels.

claim: LLM run-to-run reliability depends on setup: 42% of repeated vocabulary items changed answers across sessions (b25), but at temperature 0 large closed models rescore rubric items with ICC of .92 or more over 5 runs (d13); item-sampling reliability of benchmark composites is about .97 (d07).
agent_test: Measure run-to-run variance of our agent before comparing arms; use repeated seeds.

claim: Scaffold-level evaluation cost can fall by using sparse item sets: tinyBenchmarks 100 items per scenario about 2% error; metabench under 3% of items, 1.24% RMSE.
agent_test: Use small IRT-selected item sets to compare schema arms cheaply.

claim: Inference-heavy reasoning models raise only some ability dimensions (quantitative and logical reasoning, relevance filtering, mind modelling) while knowledge dimensions follow model size (ADeLe, 15 LLMs; o1 and R1-distilled vs others).
agent_test: Compare the scaffold arm and the plain arm per demand dimension; expect gains on reasoning demands, none on knowledge-limited items. No same-model scaffold vs plain factor study exists.

claim: Demand-profile predictors keep working on new tasks (AUROC 0.81) and new benchmarks (0.75) for a fixed model, but per-item scaffold benefit at equal tokens has not been measured.
agent_test: Run the first per-item scaffold-gain regression on demand levels ourselves.

claim: Family and duplicate covariance is not the source of the LLM general factor: first component 73.5% on all 4,575 leaderboard models and 71.6-73.9% with one per organisation (own computation).
agent_test: Report g share with one-model-per-family resampling; do not cite one g number without sample design.

claim: No clear second factor is visible among open-model leaderboard scores except an instruction-following axis (PC2 12.3%, IFEval versus MUSR); a separable reasoning factor in Burnell is not reproduced where tests are mostly multiple choice.
agent_test: Test the reasoning factor with open-ended tasks, not multiple-choice.

claim: Carroll himself doubted that g is more than a statistical product after 1993, and Horn denied g; the g versus broad-abilities debate was never closed even inside the Carroll-Horn line.
agent_test: Use g as a descriptive index of the benchmark manifold only.
